findings.title: M4.6e's own row still states the REMOVED depth cap as this task's termination mechanism
findings.failure_scenario: The staged M4.6e row reads: '⚠️ TRANSITIVE across several terms, and bounded -- a CONTINUE may only ever name a LOWER epoch, so a chain deeper than 1000 is corrupt bytes rather than long history and stops loudly rather than recursing until the stack goes.' Every clause is now false. There is no depth cap: `MAX_CHAIN_DEPTH` is gone, and the only `1000`s left in ChainReplay are LIST page sizes plus one correctly-worded historical note at line 131. A chain deeper than 1000 is NOT corrupt -- measured on this staged tree, 1002 and 20000 legitimate terms both recover with the correct offset. And the justification is the same non-sequitur found in round 1: strictly-decreasing epochs bound depth by the EPOCH NUMBER, which is what makes a 1000 cap wrong rather than what makes it right. The code and the tests were both corrected (ChainReplay.java:129-135, CommitLogCrossEpochTest.java:189-193 each say plainly that the cap was false and why); only the row that is the permanent record of what this task built was not. Concrete harm, and it is a regression path rather than a reading nuisance: the backlog is authoritative and is what the next agent consults, so someone reconciling the row against the code sees a documented safety mechanism that is absent and restores it -- re-introducing the defect measured in round 1, where at 1002 terms every node's `start` threw, released the lease, and the cluster could never elect a sequencer again while being told its correct history was corrupt bytes. It is major rather than minor for the additional reason that round 2 reported this claim as 'gone from both the code and the backlog row' and it is present in the staged bytes: a correction asserted rather than made, which is the same shape as the R2 numbers, in the same file, one row away. ⚠️ Secondary, same row and same edit: '⚠️ Epoch 0 is not followed ... the guard sits on the CROSSING rather than on the walk' describes the round-1 recursive design -- there is no longer a `crossFrom` in ChainReplay; the guard is now `inherited`'s `prevEpoch >= 1` at ChainReplay.java:76 plus the hop-add tests inside `replayAncestry`. The behavioural claim is still true; the mechanism named is not. And the row nowhere mentions the iterative rewrite, the strictly-lower termination check, the never-opened-chain reconstruction, or the transitive cost -- which is the substance of what the task now delivers.

findings.title: The origin exclusion is correct, but its stated justification covers only one of the two callers of replayAncestry
findings.failure_scenario: You asked me to check this rather than take it, so: the asymmetry is right as built and I could not break it. `replayAncestry` has two entry points, and `neverOpened`'s javadoc argues the exclusion for one of them -- `replay`, where the origin is the log's OWN chain and empty is the normal pre-open state. At the other, `inherited`, the origin is the PREDECESSOR chain, where empty is not normal at all and the exclusion silently yields no offsets. Measured: with chain 1 holding 100 records at [CONTINUE, delta] and chain 2 absent, `new CommitLog(store, "bins", 3).open(2, 0)` returns nextOffset 0, not 42 -- the walk stops at the origin and the history is dropped without a sound. That is unreachable today, and I checked the path rather than assuming it: `LocalSequencer.start` always runs `predecessor.seal(...)` before `log.open(...)`, and every `seal` route leaves at least a Seal at slot 0 (the `sealedAt` early return only fires when `recoverChainEnd` already found one), so `inherited`'s origin is never empty. The finding is that the safety of a guard in ChainReplay rests entirely on an ordering invariant maintained in a different class, and nothing at the guard says so. M4.6d is about to route production through `Sequencer` and M5 adds forwarding; a future path that opens without sealing first -- a fast-path takeover for a known-dead predecessor, or a recovery helper -- gets silent offset reassignment from 0 with `atOrigin` true, no exception, and no failing test. Cheapest close is to make the two callers distinguishable rather than sharing one flag, or to have `inherited` throw on an empty origin, since empty there means the invariant broke and returning no offsets is the I2-violating outcome.
